summary: John's 3rd-great-grandmother; a divorced working nurse of Plymouth who won her divorce and took back her maiden name - praised in 1893 as bearing 'a name beyond reproach'.
bio:
Catherine Scott was born at Kingston on 14 May 1837 (Bradsby), 'the third' of six living children of Stephen and Julia Ann Scott; FamilySearch (LHCS-RCM) gives 2 May 1838 and the tree 1836/1837. She was 14 in the 1850 Kingston census (3 Aug 1850). She married Andrew Pringle in 1857 and had seven children. She later sued for divorce - 'the action commenced by her and sustained by the court' - and resumed her maiden name, though she was 'better known by the name of Pringle than Scott'. By 1893 she was a working nurse in Plymouth, a member of the Christian Church, owned a house and lot, had raised her children, and Bradsby wrote that she 'has always had, and now bears, a name beyond reproach... carries on her business with marked ability'. He listed five living children: John (m. Regina Stires), Ellen (m. Francis Randell), Samuel, Orange and Estella - omitting Addison. In 1910 she lived with her son Orange at Larksville. FamilySearch gives her death as 3 Sep 1918 at Larksville, buried 6 Sep 1918 in the Dallas area; the tree shows 1910 as her death year (conflict; 1918 preferred, as she is in the 1910 census).

Catherine's death is now confirmed from the state index: the 1918 Pennsylvania death index lists 'Pringle, Catherine', file 100575, Larksville, 3 September 1918 ([R4-S1]). She died under her married name, although Bradsby says she had resumed 'Scott' after her divorce. The two later censuses show her living with her son Orange: in June 1900 in Plymouth Township, where she is recorded as divorced, the mother of seven children of whom five were living, with her son Addison's family in the next house and probably her daughter Ella Randall one house further ([R4-S2]); and in April 1910 at Larksville, where she is a widow, aged 71 ([R4-S3]).

The 1910 entry is the first record to say where her parents were born: both in Connecticut ([R4-S3]). That disagrees with the 1850 census (Stephen and Julia Ann both b. Pa.) and the 1900 census (parents b. Pa.), but agrees with Bradsby's 1893 statement, given while Julia Ann was alive, that Stephen and Julia were both born in Connecticut. The question of a Connecticut origin for the Scotts and Watsons is therefore open again (see Stephen J. Scott and Julia Ann Watson). The 1910 figure of 11 children born is higher than 1900's 7; 7 is supported by the 1870 household (Ellen Jane, John, Samuel, Addison, Orange, infant Julia(n)) plus Stella.
funFacts: A divorced woman who reverted to her maiden name in the 19th century - rare at the time.
Bradsby's sketch is the only published biography of a direct Pringle-line woman.
